core_answer_facts: Tang et al. (2025, TR-C) represent demand switching by the continuous variable pi_i^{l,l'}(k), the number of passengers switching from line l to l' at source cell i in interval k; switching happens only at source cells.
In Tang et al. (2025) only shared lines (shuttle, taxi, subway, bus) exchange demand; private-car passengers (mode 5) cannot switch.
Tang et al. (2025) Eq. (8) caps total switching l->l' at a source cell at rho^{l,l'} (0-1) times the demand for l; Eq. (9) caps per-interval switched-away demand at the original demand D_i^l(k).
In Tang et al. (2025) pi enters source-cell flow conservation (Eq. 5) and line completion (Eq. 7), and objective term Z3 adds a per-passenger switching cost c_D^{l,l'} x pi (penalty/hub subsidy).
reference_answer: In Tang et al.'s joint crowd-evacuation and vehicle-scheduling MILP, demand switching is modelled by the continuous, non-negative decision variable pi_i^{l,l'}(k): the number of passengers whose preferred line is l who are reassigned to line l' at source cell i during interval k. Switching is allowed only at source cells (origin zones), i.e. before passengers start walking through the hub network, and only among shared transportation lines L_S (shuttle, taxi, subway, bus); private-car passengers (mode 5) cannot switch, and nobody switches after boarding. How many may switch is governed by two constraints: Eq. (8) caps the total switched from l to l' at source cell i over the horizon at rho^{l,l'} times the total demand for l at that cell (rho^{l,l'} in [0,1] is a parameter for the maximum switchable proportion, lower when lines overlap less or differ more in comfort/price), and Eq. (9) keeps the number switched away from l in each interval at most the original demand D_i^l(k). The variables enter the source-cell flow conservation Eq. (5) (demand for line l at the source cell becomes D_i^l(k) plus inflows switched to l minus outflows switched away from l) and the line-level completion constraint Eq. (7) (all redistributed demand of each line must eventually board that line's vehicles). The objective term Z3 adds a per-passenger switching cost c_D^{l,l'} times pi (interpretable as a hub subsidy), so switching is penalised and traded off against travel-time and vehicle-operation costs. In the solution algorithm pi is a continuous subproblem variable, and the same switching constraints reappear in the time-expanded reformulation (B.2), (B.7), (B.8).

core_answer_facts: Zhao et al. (2019, TR-B) treat the skin conductance response amplitude P as social repulsive force divided by a unit conversion factor alpha (P = F_rep/alpha).
Zhao et al. (2019) pair each crowd-passing event's Autonomate-extracted SCR amplitude with r_ij - d_ij at the minimum distance to the nearest stationary pedestrian.

Zhao et al. (2019) fit exponential (A~_i, B_i) and logistic (SCR_max, s_0, k_0) SCR-distance functions by GLS separately for walking, running and blind experiments (Table 1), e.g. walking logistic SCR_max 0.283 uS; logistic R2 higher.
Zhao et al. (2019) multiply the fitted SCR response/amplitude by alpha = 2.10 x 10^3 N/uS to obtain repulsive force; distance and slope parameters retain their own units.
reference_answer: Zhao et al. treat the measured skin conductance response (SCR) amplitude P as a proxy for the social repulsive force divided by a unit conversion factor alpha (N/uS), i.e. P = F_ij^rep / alpha. For each pass of the moving participant through the stationary crowd they build one sample point: the SCR amplitude of that event, extracted automatically with the Autonomate method (event-related window, latency 0.5-4 s, onset-to-peak <= 4 s, a minimum amplitude threshold of 0.02 uS (the text says above the threshold); only the first two samples per participant to limit habituation), paired with the interpersonal distance r_ij - d_ij taken at the minimum centre distance d_ij to the nearest stationary pedestrian (r_ij uses the lateral body width l_i cos(theta_i) to account for body twisting). These P versus r_ij - d_ij data (range -0.04 to 0.10 m) are fitted with two functional forms: the classical exponential P = A~_i e^{(r_ij-d_ij)/B_i} (Eq. 2, A~_i in uS) and a proposed logistic P = SCR_max / (1 + e^{-k_0 (r_ij - d_ij - s_0)}) (Eq. 3). The coefficients (A~_i, B_i; SCR_max, s_0, k_0) are estimated by generalized least squares separately for the walking, running and blind experiments and reported in Table 1 (e.g. walking logistic SCR_max = 0.283 uS, s_0 = 0.007 m, k_0 = 95.069 m^-1; exponential A~_i = 0.138 uS, B_i = 0.084 m); the logistic form fits better (R2 0.578/0.538/0.603 vs 0.392/0.394/0.475). The amplitude parameters A~_i and SCR_max are in uS, B_i and s_0 are in m, and k_0 is in m^-1. In the modified social force model the SCR response function's output is multiplied by alpha, set as a 'reasonable estimate' of 2.10 x 10^3 N/uS, to give the repulsive force magnitude (Eq. 7). Equivalently, alpha rescales the amplitude, not the distance parameters B_i and s_0 or the slope parameter k_0. Face-to-face/face-to-back orientation enters only through mean SCR comparisons and, in validation simulations, a smaller face-to-back SCR_max (0.085 uS) whose derivation is not detailed.

core_answer_facts: Pan 2024 ev-PINN predicts rho,phi,u,c and adds algebraic speed/cost residuals without reducing conservation derivative order.
Pan 2024 ro-PINN predicts rho,phi,qx,qy and introduces conservation plus flux consistency residuals at first derivative order.
Pan 2024 combines residual, boundary and initial losses with alpha/beta weights; printed Eq17 conflicts with Eq7 on the qy gradient coordinate.
reference_answer: Both schemes retain density rho and potential phi. ev-PINN adds speed u and cost c as network outputs and adds algebraic consistency residuals f6=u-U(rho,x,y) and f7=c-C(rho,x,y); it retains the Eikonal residual f1 and the substituted conservation residual f2, with the latter still involving second spatial derivatives. ro-PINN instead adds flow components qx and qy. Its residual set is f1 (Eikonal), f3=rho_t+(qx)_x+(qy)_y (conservation) and f4/f5 (consistency of predicted flows with the potential-gradient flux relation), using first derivatives. The paper lists the combined PDE residual terms as f1+f2+f6+f7 for ev-PINN and f1+f3+f4+f5 for ro-PINN. It defines a squared residual collocation loss in Eq9, boundary-condition losses and initial-condition losses, and combines them as Jloss=alpha Jres+beta Jbc+Jinit. Boundary penalties enforce inlet flow, wall flow and outlet potential; transient initial penalties constrain density and both flow components. Two publication caveats should be preserved: Eq17 prints phi_x in the qy residual although the defining qy relation Eq7 uses phi_y; and the later residual-sum shorthand should not be read as an unqualified new unsquared training objective overriding Eq9. Report the printed construction and inconsistency rather than silently correcting the paper or inventing an implementation.

core_answer_facts: Li 2023 Sec3.6 defines quiescence as speed below 0.1m/s and tq as the duration of that phase.
Li 2023 extracts PeTrack trajectories and applies mean smoothing before subsequent speed/behavior analysis.
reference_answer: Quiescent behavior is the phase in which a pedestrian speed is below 0.1 m/s, interpreted as a stop phase. Quiescent time tq is the duration of that low-speed state, rather than the interval between consecutive pedestrians crossing the entrance or the entire evacuation time. The authors extract trajectories with PeTrack, smooth them by a mean filter to reduce head/body sway, and conduct subsequent analyses using the smoothed trajectories together with video. Speed is calculated from coordinate changes; applying the threshold identifies the low-speed phase and its elapsed duration. The paper does not specify a separate minimum-dwell rule or gap-merging convention, so these should not be invented. Its smoothing description says about one second/50 frames and specifies Delta t=24 frames; that wording need not be silently converted into an exact 50-sample implementation.

reference_answer: The strategic layer separates leader placement from dynamic exit selection. Placement minimizes leader number M=sum_i X_i, subject to coverage of each cell containing pedestrians unable to find exits: sum_i X_i Z_i,j>=1, with X_i and Z_i,j binary (location and coverage indicators). It is not an objective directly minimizing evacuation time or hazard probability. Exit selection chooses the smallest dynamic weight W_lk=D_lk+delta P_lk/B_k. Risk is represented by Euclidean distance D_lk to the exit (longer means greater risk), while congestion is the count P_lk of pedestrians closer to exit k than the leader, normalized by exit width B_k. From the CTPF distribution, cells not guided by leader l contribute rho_i A_i when closer, and half that occupancy when equally distant. Thus risk and congestion are modeling proxies in the exit-choice score; delta controls the congestion contribution. Leader movement is subsequently simulated using a social-force model; this does not replace the placement coverage constraints.

reference_answer: A binary attention state evolves as a first-order Markov chain. Initiation and continuation/termination probabilities use polynomial logistic functions of angular separation (shop visual size) and observation angle (walking direction versus shop entrance midpoint); next state is a Bernoulli sample. While attending, desired speed is neutral speed scaled by min(ideal/current angular speed,1); ideal angular speed is sampled once per pedestrian and current angular speed concerns the display midpoint. Without attention neutral speed applies. This dynamic desired speed enters the SFM goal force, slowing near displays rather than adding a shop-attraction force.

core_answer_facts: Nicolas 2017 defines exit capacity as crossings per unit time and specific capacity as capacity per metre width.

reference_answer: The corpus distinguishes empirical exit throughput (people crossing an exit per unit time), its width-normalized specific capacity, and a fundamental-diagram proxy (the peak flow of an ordinary unidirectional stream). Nicolas et al. describe tabulated observational or controlled-experiment values and warn that the fundamental-diagram peak can underestimate doorway capacity. Passage-time/counting methods estimate N/T, whereas width normalization reports throughput per metre of width and assumes an approximately linear width relation. Liao et al. distinguish all-run mean throughput from steady-state throughput: their modified CUSUM identifies stable density and speed intervals, uses their overlap to select the flow interval, and then computes passage-count flow. These are different estimation windows and normalizations, not interchangeable universal maxima. Supply, geometry and pedestrian behavior must be stated; density/speed stabilize the interval rather than automatically establishing a capacity from arbitrary rho-v products.

core_answer_facts: Pouw 2024 contrasts fixed-area hydrodynamic density, Voronoi cells and a bounded personal-space union estimator.
The Lyon field dataset 2025 describes Gaussian spatial and temporal coarse graining from trajectories.
Tian 2012 uses entrance/exit-time fractional occupancy to reduce narrow-region fluctuations.
Nicolas 2017 reports similar preliminary results for a slightly larger rectangular region than its semicircular doorway zone.
reference_answer: The corpus describes several trajectory/position based estimators: count pedestrians in a fixed region and divide by its area; assign inverse Voronoi-cell area at each position (and average spatially if needed); smooth discrete positions into a density field using a normalized Gaussian kernel, optionally followed by time averaging; interpolate effective occupancy from entrance/exit times in a narrow corridor measurement section; and divide observed occupancy by the union of bounded personal-space regions clipped to the observation region. Pouw et al. note that fixed-region counting depends strongly on area size and averages out local fluctuations; sparse Voronoi cells need boundary clipping or thresholds. Tian et al. report large fluctuations in a narrow region and use entrance/exit interpolation to reduce them. Nicolas et al. balance locality and noise with a small semicircular exit zone and report similar preliminary results for a slightly larger rectangular zone. This is a particular size/shape comparison, not evidence that geometry never matters. Gaussian bandwidth, temporal averaging and personal-space/boundary choices define the resolution of their estimators.

atoms.anchor_text: Fruin proposed one of the earliest approaches to classify congestion in pedestrian crowds (Fruin et al., 1987). Using the Level of Service (LOS) different types of facilities are rated on a scale from A (not crowded) to F (unacceptable overly crowded condition) based on qualitative remarks. Fruin also provides numerical values for density and flow expected at each LOS, but numbers change from facility to facility. The LOS has the advantage of being very practical and since it covers a variety of facilities, it can be considered a versatile definition of congestion levels. In addition, it is constantly updated and it also considers particular cases such as crosswalks (zebra crossings) or escalators (Transportation, 2016). However, the LOS is not universal and an implementation in the frame of real-time crowd control would be difficult. [...] Helbing et al. (2007) proposed a “crowd pressure” defined as the local variance of velocity multiplied by the corresponding density.
atoms.conditions: Facility-specific LOS; density alone insufficient

The average velocity vector for the cell being considered results from the average of the vectors contained within that cell. We found that a mesh size of 0.2 m and a sampling time interval of 2.5 s are the best combination, which allows to obtain accurate results and ensure an adequate space and spatial resolution.

reference_answer: Supported indicator families include: density/LOS (counts or individual locations and usable area, facility-specific flow/space criteria); crowd pressure (local density times local velocity variance, requiring trajectories/velocity samples and density); congestion level CL (local signed-curl range divided by mean speed from gridded velocity vectors with specified mesh, sampling window and ROI); crowd danger (CL times local density); dimensionless congestion number CN (differential congestion normalized by extreme differential congestion, requiring the velocity/curl field plus ROI/body-scale normalization); and model-estimated physical contact force/stress (configuration/contact geometry, velocities, mass/inertia and constitutive/contact constraints). These are distinct from one another: trajectory crowd pressure is not mechanical force or a validated fatality probability. No single threshold or indicator alone establishes crush safety.

reference_answer: Direct speed–density evidence is provided by Zhang and Jia (2021): they extend density-only Drake/Greenshields-type relations with a separate conflicting-stream density term. In the extended form, total density alone need not determine walking speed; the conflict parameter controls the extra effect, and setting it to zero recovers the corresponding baseline. Parameters were fitted to speed and density samples extracted from the bidirectional BFR-DML-360 video trajectories. The selected extended linear form fit slightly better than the density-only linear form (reported R² 0.99955 versus 0.99952), and the authors associate the extra opposing-stream effect with lane formation. This is evidence from comparing fitted speed–density models on a bidirectional dataset, not a matched experimental estimate of a universal bidirectional speed penalty. As optional context, Jin et al. report comparable or sometimes higher bidirectional throughput at comparable densities in periodic ring corridors after lane formation. Those flow–density measurements, and the capacity differences summarized by the bidirectional-capacity review, cannot by themselves establish a mean-speed–density difference. The corpus examples therefore need to be reported with their metric, lane organization, geometry and evidence type intact.

reference_answer: Models encode following as conditional social information rather than an invariant follow-the-majority rule. Haghani/Sarvi’s exit-choice logits distinguish flow towards visible versus invisible exits, alongside distance/queue/visibility; visible heavy flows can be avoided while invisible-exit flows attract. Exit-choice revision also uses recent peer changes (SocInf) in a binary logit. These choice coefficients are empirically calibrated from individual experimental decisions, with reported estimates for high urgency and uncalibrated defaults separately marked. Lovreglio et al. model the probability of selecting the most crowded exit by random-utility/logit methods using personal/environmental predictors; calibration is stated-choice online survey data, with follow-up interviews probing social influence, not revealed dangerous-evacuation behavior. That paper reviews deterministic and stochastic herding assumptions, but its own fitted coefficients are survey-based. Another complete example is the CellEVAC follower model: a binary social-influence variable and changes in the nearby leader’s recommendation enter exit-choice revision. Its first four revision coefficients are adopted from Haghani and Sarvi; the added leader-change coefficient was selected by simulation search. Environmental exit-choice coefficients were re-estimated from a filtered Haghani choice dataset, while leader influence remained configurable. Reusing those observations is not an independent replication.

reference_answer: Bottleneck discharge rates can provide a conditional starting point, not a validated clearance prediction for this station. Liao et al. show that transient and steady-state throughput can differ; a short train-arrival surge need not spend enough time in the regime used to measure capacity. Width alone does not specify initial crowd size, density, behavior or geometry. Li et al. explicitly excluded luggage from their bottleneck trials. Haghani reports luggage-related single-file findings (larger headways, reduced acceleration and a lower-density FD stable point), but these are a review of another study and not a measured luggage correction for this door. Geoerg et al. explicitly leave transfer of assistive-device effects to luggage unresolved. Therefore do not multiply an unrestricted specific flow by 1.2 m and assert that each surge clears. As a dimensional and queueing inference, rather than a formula quoted from Liao, a queue/discharge calculation requires at least passengers per surge, spacing of surges, residual queue and a defensible time-dependent discharge rate for the luggage mix; a constant-rate N/q calculation is only an assumption for a continuously supplied queue and excludes startup/arrival spread. The provided inputs cannot yield a numerical yes/no clearance result. Local matched measurements or a validated calibration would be needed.

core_answer_facts: Wu et al. explicitly condition logit alternatives and potential computation on facility-layout familiarity, using known exits, φ and θ.
Wu’s observations concern 481 people normally leaving Beijing’s Zhichun Road station via stairs or escalator; familiarity is inferred from immediate/hesitant/reselecting behavior.
The model is empirically fitted and checked within that station setting; this is not a mall main/side-door or emergency-transfer validation.
Boundedly rational full-familiarity assumptions and CellEVAC optimization remain optional contrasts, not evidence that the corpus lacks familiarity-sensitive implementations.
input_sufficiency_note: Sufficient for the explicit contextual applicability question. A numerical prediction for the hypothetical target would require additional inputs; the question does not require that calculation.
reference_answer: Yes, at least one implemented corpus model explicitly represents familiarity, but its empirical setting is only a limited analogue for the mall. Wu et al. model facility-layout familiarity through which exits a pedestrian knows and through different potential-field calculations for familiar and unfamiliar pedestrians. Their exit-choice logit normalizes over known exits; familiar pedestrians are assumed to know all exits, while unfamiliar pedestrians know some through guide signs. A familiar-population share φ and an expectation weight θ for hidden-route conditions enter the model. This is facility knowledge and anticipated route conditions, not an independently fitted habit preference for a previously used main door over an equally known side door. The empirical case is normal leaving at Beijing’s Zhichun Road subway station: 481 pedestrians choose the directly visible stairway (Exit 2) or continue towards the escalator (Exit 1). Immediate choosers are described as possibly familiar, while hesitation and reselection supply the other behavioral classes. Familiarity was inferred from observed choice behavior, rather than independently measured prior experience. The authors impose observed entrance flow and the inferred familiarity composition in simulations, tune a parameter against stair choices and fit θ against observed stairway flows, with a within-setting consistency check. These are genuine empirical calibration steps, but they do not validate emergency shopping-mall main/side-exit shares. Optional contrasts remain useful: the boundedly rational model assumes everyone knows the scenario, and CellEVAC’s chosen utility/persistence attributes do not encode prior familiarity and were optimized rather than fitted to real/survey data. A mall application would need measured exit awareness or prior use, visibility/signage, relative route disutilities and matched calibration. No station stair-choice percentage should be relabelled as a mall side-exit prediction, and the old negative examples cannot establish that familiarity-sensitive models are absent from the corpus.

Hänseler et al. use a TU Berlin entrance-hall crossing at roughly 90 degrees, with a reported maximum density of 5 persons/m² and mainly student pedestrians. The anisotropic stream-based model better captures route differences, but the crossing case parameters were calibrated on the full data set and residual individual variability is substantial. This provides usable model/data structure for estimating each stream once local geometry, inflows, densities, composition and a baseline are supplied; peak hour alone is not a numerical density specification. reference_answer: The corpus has decision-relevant outcomes, but matching exit width alone is insufficient. Chen et al. used a 1 m exit with 97 mainly university-student participants and double S-shaped guardrails, comparing with no obstacles. They measured exit timing/headways/flow and spatial density; rails prolonged evacuation while limiting maximum area density. These are not a single column or a demonstrated 500-person hall result. Zanlungo et al. show repeated bottleneck drills with and without a round obstacle at a 0.75 m exit; density and congestion-number maxima move to the obstacle sides, and density and unstable-motion maxima need not coincide. This bears on where crowding occurs but is not an outflow improvement estimate. Haghani’s secondary synthesis reports mixed findings for columns/panels: its human laboratory rows report effects of size, distance and exit location on outflow, as well as pressure relief without a change in total evacuation time. Its animal/insect rows must be distinguished from direct human evidence. The operator should compare obstacle-free and specified column placement using both outflow and local crowding measures. The proposed column diameter, setback/lateral gap and crowd conditions are unspecified, and the reviewed examples do not establish their effect at the joint 1 m/500-person setting. No universal beneficial-column conclusion follows.

atoms.anchor_text: As shown in Fig. 8, the flows in the three experiments are all linearly dependent on bottleneck width. We choose a linear regression y = k · x (see Eq. (2)). Since Js = ρ · v, the specific flow concept gives J = Js · W. Here W is the bottleneck width b. Note that bottleneck width b = 0.4 m is the minimum width for pedestrians to pass. Thus, the regression line for b smaller than 0.4 m has no physical meaning with respect to pedestrian flow. The fitting degree is evaluated by the coefficient of determination R2 (see Appendix C), which ranges from 0 to 1. The linearity fits the best when R2 = 1. In Fig. 8 all the values of R2 are above 0.880 (see Table C.1), which indicates that the linearity is relatively reliable. reference_answer: The corpus supports a conditional linear approximation over tested settings, not a universal flow-width law. Liao et al. reanalyze cooperative, purposeful walking without haste: EG tested ten widths from 0.9 to 2.5 m, AO five from 2.4 to 5.0 m, and UO three sets spanning 0.7 to 2.0 m. These are discrete settings, not continuous exhaustive validation. Their fitted flow-width relations are linear within these groups, but the slopes can change between all-state and steady-state selection. The experiments also differ in geometry. Nicolas et al. summarize earlier evidence for approximate proportional scaling and a stepwise alternative based on only two widths; that is secondary discussion, not an additional independently verified experiment here. Li et al. tested able-bodied, luggage-free adults instructed to run as if there were a fire, in a 45-degree funnel with widths 0.60–1.65 m in 0.15-m steps. Their results paragraph reports increasing specific flow with increasing width for running, in contrast to the approximately constant specific flow discussed for ordinary walking. This comparison spans different treatments and geometries and does not isolate a universal causal geometry effect. Geoerg et al. explicitly limit their heterogeneous-crowd experiment to free-flow conditions below 3 persons/m² that do not reach geometric capacity, with emergency transfer untested. A defensible linear approximation must therefore retain the tested geometry, population, behavioral regime and averaging window; these examples do not establish one transferable slope outside those conditions.

atoms.anchor_text: internal validity of a crowd experiment refers to the extent to which the experiment can reveal genuine causal relations (or the extent to which it can reveal the absence of causal relationship). Maximising this feature of a crowd experiment could often necessitate abstraction, simplification and exertion of high levels of experimental control. External validity of a crowd experiment, on the other hand, concerns the extent of generalisability of findings to the contexts beyond the experiment setting. Often, these two features of a crowd experiment could conflict and create a trade-off. This conflict and its implications on experiment design as well as interpretation and assessment of experimental findings in crowd dynamics essentially constitutes the main motivation of this work. Enhancing external validity of experiments often can only come at the cost of compromising internal validity and losing experimental control, and vice versa. In other words, in vast majority of cases, the investigator cannot maintain high levels of both dimensions at the same time. The more the investigator controls for extraneous factors, the more he/she relinquishes the ability to generalise the findings to a broader context. Therefore, it would be essential to consciously recognise the dimension of validity (i.e., internal or external) that matters the most to each investigation and tailor the design of the experiment accordingly.

reference_answer: The compared outputs are model- and test-specific. Haghani and Sarvi calibrate their operational social-force coefficients by minimizing discrepancies in total bottleneck evacuation time; decision modules use disaggregate exit-choice, exit-choice-change and reaction-time observations under the selected high-urgency regime. A comparison targeted at total evacuation time does not, by itself, validate every simulated trajectory or density pattern. Xiao et al. compare SFM and heuristics-model trajectories with empirical circle-antipode experiments using fundamental-diagram, speed/direction choice, travel-time and route-length distributions, distance-to-start/destination time series and trajectory-pattern indexes. A model can agree in local dynamic reaction while missing detours or reproducing different speed/route distributions. Agreement on a fitted total time or another selected output therefore supports that tested observable under its calibration conditions, not automatic accuracy of individual paths, density hotspots or untested scenarios. Calibration to the same data is not an independent predictive test. This limit is inferred from the documented calibration targets and the internal/external-validity distinction; it is not a separate predictive test. Output-specific evaluation under the intended new conditions is needed before making broader claims.

atoms.anchor_text: This tendency of participants to modify their behaviour because they are being watched by the researchers constitutes the threat of Hawthorn effect to external validity. Another example could be an experiment where participants realised (as a result of the investigators accidently sharing the information with them during the brief or through participants inferring from other cues) that investigators are interested in their decision changing behaviour during evacuations [94]. This may prompt them to change their decision more often than they naturally do, just to appease the investigator and give them the data that they need. This is also sometimes referred to as experimenter/investigator bias when participants modify their behaviour in order to provide the desired outcome, by trying to infer or guess the underlying purpose of the experiment. reference_answer: Controlled instructed egress can establish how measured flow and behavior change under its defined treatments, test specific hypotheses and calibrate selected model components, provided confounds and instruction/construct validity are addressed. That is useful evidence; absence of genuine danger does not by itself invalidate an experiment. But it does not establish the prevalence or magnitude of behavior under real life-threatening conditions. Nicolas et al. explicitly define evacuation as emptying a room and exclude panic, high pressure, violence and extreme haste, studying limited pushing and prescribed polite/selfish behavior. Haghani emphasizes that internal validity and contextual/population generalization differ and that awareness of observation or investigator expectations can alter behavior. Real-incident video evidence complements experiments but is itself selectively sampled, off-camera incomplete and correlational. Consequently neither an instructed treatment nor a naturally occurring observation alone warrants a universal claim about actual-emergency aggression, route choices or discharge. Generalization should retain geometry, population, density, motivation and threat conditions, triangulate methods and test external validity; a model parameter or treatment effect is not proof that real crowds behave that way.

However, note that this is an estimate valid for comparison purposes, but that in no case does it allow a precise determination of the actual probability of accidents occurring.

core_answer_facts: Zhang/Jia, CellEVAC and distance-keeping MPC report simulated controller effects; empirical calibration and the simulated DeployE setting do not establish field effectiveness.

Controlled human intervention evidence includes Chen’s 97-person guardrails, Yi’s 17-person queueing, Haghani/Yazdani’s 120 recruits in 60-person trials, and Bode’s 2013 crossing data; within-paper simulations and reused batches must remain distinguishable.

reference_answer: The corpus-wide predominant method remains unresolved in this revision: the 106-source method ledger is not yet a fully adjudicated, deduplicated study census. The verified intervention evidence contains several distinct methods. Zhang and Jia's inflow control, CellEVAC/leader-following guidance and distance-keeping MPC are evaluated in computer simulations. Empirical model calibration does not establish field effectiveness, and the MPC paper's Deployment environment is itself a simulator; the related prediction-model paper leaves real-crowd controller testing to future work. Controlled human evidence is substantial enough that it must be represented explicitly. Chen's 97-volunteer guardrail experiment found longer evacuation time for the small crowd and maximum area density no greater than without obstacles. Yi's 17-person experiment tested queueing instructions, with a separate model-based extension. Haghani and Yazdani recruited 120 people, tested subgroups of 60 and found mostly insignificant handholding effects but consistent clearance-time improvement from line formation under the tested conditions and full compliance. Bode and colleagues reanalysed two days of human crossing experiments: roundabout instructions and a central column changed some movement patterns but did not change facility capacity. The Love Parade paper provides qualitative real-event reconstruction rather than a controlled intervention-effect estimate. These results support intervention-, geometry-, demand- and compliance-specific statements about simulated or measured flow, density, order and evacuation performance. They do not by themselves establish general injury-risk reductions; the leader-guidance paper explicitly limits its pressure-based safety measure to comparison rather than precise accident probability. A field-versus-simulation majority, a robust change in that majority under broader inclusion, and a corpus-wide staged-release gap are not asserted while eligibility, research batches and shared-data/model lineages remain unresolved.

atoms.anchor_text: However, it is important to remark that real measurements of pedestrian properties result in a number of dots dispersed over a large surface roughly defining the behavior indicated as a line in Fig 1. Therefore, clearly determining if a given flow configuration has to be considered congested may become difficult by using the FD alone. For example, Zhang et al. [19] found that fundamental diagrams for unidirectional and bidirectional flow are different. In addition, while the definition of capacity and critical density appears as a single and unique point in the representation of Fig 1, in reality, transition to congestion occurs at a range of densities. In brief, capacity is a rather simple definition from a theoretical perspective, but defining it in practical terms becomes much more difficult. As we will see in the next section, for the bidirectional case considered here the flow ratio plays a central role when investigating the transition to congestion. [...] Finally, it should be also noted that, in the case of simulation, the deadlock concept is very often used. Some authors used simulations to study the density at which the “jamming transition” occurs, i.e. the density at which deadlocks occur and pedestrians cannot cross the corridor at all. Although this type of studies are important to develop better simulation models, the relation with reality is uncertain since deadlocks almost never occur in real situations and a minimal flow was reported also under very extreme conditions [18, 20, 21] (the origin and nature of this minimum flow is not clear). Therefore, although we will often refer to deadlock occurrence as a phase transition while reviewing simulation models, it is important to remind that this concept do not necessarily applies to real situations

[pearl-src-fc7375ffc5f94a19] The wide-track capacity peak near 2.5 ped/m² and body-contact change near 6 ped/m² coexist with no typical stop-and-go waves in that setting.
[pearl-src-2c6f1c912f4d8ceb] Ring-flow statistics are robust over the stated subarea/time-window changes, but this is not a validated jam-onset invariance result.

reference_answer: The evidence supports condition-specific operational markers, but these must not be relabeled as one measurement-independent density at which pedestrian flow becomes unstable or jammed. The bidirectional-capacity synthesis distinguishes the fundamental-diagram maximum (critical/capacity density) from a theoretical zero-flow jam density and notes that observed transition is spread over a density range. Jin et al.'s wide-track experiment reports a capacity peak near 2.5 ped/m² and a separate body-contact transition near 6 ped/m². The latter accompanies a change in the decreasing-flow branch; it is not an observed universal standstill or stop-and-go onset. In that 1.5 m wide-track unidirectional setting typical stop-and-go waves did not emerge, whereas the single-file experiment showed them in an intermediate-density regime. The same paper cites prior method comparisons with similar averaged values but different standard deviations; this is secondary support for mean comparability, not an onset test. Measurement robustness is also conditional: the follow-up ring-corridor analysis reports consistent statistics for 6–10 subareas and 10–20 s intervals. That is positive evidence for those processing choices, not invariance to every density estimator or validation of a jam-onset number. Nicolas et al. summarize prior spatial/temporal averaging differences, and Liao's direct bottleneck reanalysis shows that all-state and steady-state flow estimates differ. The ring-corridor authors also explicitly distinguish flow-rate fluctuations from stop-and-go waves and leave quantitative stability across densities for further testing. Force-based-model stability analysis adds a separate warning: mathematically unstable regimes can produce backward motion and overlap instead of realistic jams. Thus any claimed threshold must specify its physical endpoint, geometry, direction mix, density convention, averaging and stationarity definition. The reviewed evidence does not turn the reported 2.5 or 6 ped/m² markers into a method-robust instability or jamming trigger.

[pearl-src-b40f5056a160d4e9] Φ has a nonzero random baseline depending on direction ratio and finite grid width, restricting raw cross-configuration comparisons.
[pearl-src-2c6f1c912f4d8ceb] Ring-corridor radial mean/spread stabilization and snapshots define lane formation and TLF without a universal numerical tolerance in the cited passage.
reference_answer: Lane formation is represented by several operational observables. In the bidirectional-capacity study, cells with the same x-velocity direction define lanes, empty cells are ignored, and the lane-count mean and variation are measured along the corridor. Those counts alone can misclassify a chessboard-like configuration. The study therefore also defines row-wise direction segregation, its global average Φ, and a composite disorganization measure Var(Nlanes)/(Avg(Nlanes)·Φ). The random baseline for Φ depends on the flow ratio and the number of grid columns, so the same raw Φ is not automatically comparable across configurations. This study uses several supervised datasets with similar acquisition/geometrical arrangements but different experimental procedures. As another example, Jin et al. use the direction-specific mean and sample standard deviation of radial positions in a ring corridor; stabilization of those series, interpreted with snapshots, marks the lane-formation process and its duration TLF. This is a different observable and geometry, and the cited passage does not specify a universal numerical tolerance for stabilization. These measures can be used as model-validation targets if experiment and model share the definition, trajectory processing, spatial grid or radial convention, observation window, geometry, density and directional/instruction conditions. That is a conditional validation recommendation inferred from the operational definitions and their stated limitations, not evidence that one interchangeable lane scalar validates every counterflow scenario.

atoms.anchor_text: In summary, we have performed pedestrian flow experiments through a 72-cm-wide door, in which a (variable) fraction c ⋆ s of the participants were asked to behave selfishly, while the rest behaved politely. Irrespective of these behaviours, a first series of experiments was conducted with placid walkers and a second one with hurried walkers. By re-injecting egressing participants into the room, we managed to improve the statistics. Furthermore, despite instantaneous fluctuations, the pedestrian flow was found to be quasi-stationary at the macroscopic scale, unlike in other experiments ( Seyfried et al., 2009a; Garcimartín et al., 2016 ). The flow rate J gets higher for larger c ⋆ s and with more hurried walkers. The absence of a ‘faster-is-slower’ effect does not contradict its possible occurrence ( Garcimartín et al., 2014; Pastor et al., 2015 ) when one considers crowds above a competitiveness threshold.

core_answer_facts: [pearl-src-bae14f716cb901cf] Table 5 is an empirical review reporting positive human and other-system FIS evidence alongside conditional/contrary human results; it is secondary evidence.
[pearl-src-15c1100e05ee58e4] The direct 72-cm doorway experiment reports greater global flow for more selfish/hurried walking under limited conditions, not a universal no-FIS claim.
[pearl-src-c855476d71620c33] Maity et al. label a cross-model speed/evacuation-time contrast FIS; it is neither measured human panic nor an isolated within-model drive-response experiment.
reference_answer: Yes, the corpus contains reports of a faster-is-slower effect, but the provenance and conditions matter. Haghani's empirical review lists positive laboratory-human evidence, including Garcimartín et al. (2014), and reports Pastor et al.'s findings for humans, sheep and grains. Those are secondary reports in a corpus review, not primary verification here of every cited experiment; Table 5 is not a set of independent replications. The same table includes mixed or contrary laboratory results: effects depending on the number of participants, shorter discharge when rushing involves no dangerous pressure or explicit aggressive pushing, and faster-is-faster under slow running. The review explains that competition/aggression differences can account for apparently opposing findings, and explicitly excludes numerical studies from that table comparison. A direct corpus experiment by Nicolas et al., using a 72-cm door, polite/selfish instructions and placid/hurried walkers, found higher global flow with more selfish or hurried participants. It excluded extreme panic, violence, high pressure and extreme haste; extrapolation to extreme emergencies remains unresolved. Separately, Maity et al. interpret their numerical AR/PW/ARZ comparison as FIS: AR has higher speed than its equilibrium relation in dense regions yet the longest overall evacuation time. This is numerical, cross-model evidence and does not isolate the effect of increasing desired speed or pushing within one unchanged model. Thus the reviewed evidence supports conditional occurrences, not a rule that any increase in walking speed must reduce outflow. Report the evidence type, behavioral/contact treatment, geometry and outcome; whole-evacuation time and local outflow should not be conflated.

[pearl-src-b40f5056a160d4e9; pearl-src-41c7d913c29687f3; pearl-src-2c6f1c912f4d8ceb] Method descriptions alone do not establish common numeric speed/density uncertainty without temporal/spatial processing and occlusion/error checks.
reference_answer: The studies report useful acquisition and correction information, but with uneven quantitative precision evidence. The bidirectional-capacity analysis states that PeTrack can achieve positional accuracy up to 1 cm depending on cameras and markers; this is a conditional capability statement, not a measured error distribution for every trajectory. Li et al.’s funnel-bottleneck study reports intrinsic/extrinsic and scene calibration to correct distortion and smooths head-position trajectories before speed/density analysis. Jin et al. instead report manual Tracker extraction because automatic tracking had many errors. Li's printed smoothing description also needs clarification: it calls 1 s 50 frames but specifies Δt = 24 with a 2Δt+1-sample window. This source ambiguity is not an error estimate. These details help judge method quality and whether systematic distortion or tracking errors were addressed. They do not by themselves establish numerical uncertainty of derived speeds/densities: differentiation depends on time step and smoothing, while local density depends on area definition, position/boundary assignments and missing or occluded tracks. The reviewed method passages do not supply a common per-dataset occlusion/error-propagation budget. Consequently one can assess relative credibility and processing conventions, but cannot assign all reported speed/density values a universal precision from a software accuracy claim. A rigorous numerical assessment would require calibration residuals/ground-truth checks, gap/occlusion handling and the actual derivative/density computation with uncertainty propagation.

atoms.anchor_text: similar densities have been reached in controlled experiments under safe conditions (Nicholson and Roebuck, 1995; Oberhagemann, 2012; Sieben et al., 2017) [...] The above remarks raise doubts on whether density alone can be used to measure the intrinsic risk of human crowds. One of the reasons limiting the capability of density to explain the dynamics of crowd accidents lies in its static nature. As different studies noted (Helbing et al., 2007; Helbing and Mukerji, 2012), crowds become particularly dangerous when shock waves propagate, thus creating an alternation of large forces coming from multiple directions. As a consequence, while pedestrian density is important to grasp the scale of the forces acting on human body, the way in which those forces act also need to be considered. [...] Fruin also provides numerical values for density and flow expected at each LOS, but numbers change from facility to facility.
atoms.conditions: Conceptual/synthesis argument for crushing-related risk; safe high-density examples are cited prior studies, not newly observed injury validation in this atom.

atoms.anchor_text: The definition of the congestion level given above allows to determine the organizational degree of crowds and their dynamical nature. However, density needs also to be included to account for statical aspects in order to get the whole picture representing the intrinsic risk of the crowd.
atoms.conditions: Rationale for combining dynamic congestion and static density; not an empirically calibrated universal injury probability.

atoms.anchor_text: In the original work (Feliciani and Nishinari, 2018b), it is argued that a crowd moving in normal conditions (i.e., not in a state of fear or emergency, such as when trying to escape a fire) would never exceed a CLof 15 m−1. Although this value was obtained by extrapolation from experimental data, it remains a hypothesis and it would be difficult to demonstrate the existence of a limit experimentally due to safety and ethical limitations. As such, a general, universal and preferentially theoretical argument is required to demonstrate such a limit and quantify it numerically.
atoms.conditions: Critique refers to the earlier CL bound of 15 m−1, not to density, and does not dismiss all properties of the later congestion number.

core_answer_facts: [pearl-src-6bbceb8663aa0757] Comparable high density may occur in safely controlled movement; danger also depends on dynamical forces and organization.
[pearl-src-6bbceb8663aa0757] Density plus dynamical congestion and facility-specific context is more informative than one universal density cutoff.
[pearl-src-6bbceb8663aa0757; pearl-src-df9bec9b2e281134] Neither a density alert nor an extrapolated congestion bound establishes universal injury/safety prediction.
reference_answer: The corpus does not justify treating one density cutoff as a general danger indicator across settings. Density is relevant to crowd compression and available space, but it is static: Feliciani and Nishinari contrast similar high densities in safe controlled/event conditions with dangerous crowds in which shock waves and forces from changing directions matter. They therefore combine dynamical congestion with density rather than using density alone, and note that facility-specific LOS values vary. A density alert may be useful for a specified facility/measurement convention, but it neither proves injury danger above the value nor guarantees safety below it. The evidence therefore motivates assessment of the motion and force context alongside the density and facility; this is a bounded methodological inference, not a validated universal injury predictor. The later congestion-number paper also cautions that an earlier proposed universal congestion limit was extrapolated and remained a hypothesis; such alternative indicators should not be relabeled as empirically validated universal injury thresholds. The warranted conclusion is context-specific monitoring and validation, not an invariant dangerous density or certainty that every dense crowd is unsafe.

atoms.anchor_text: The comparison of data provided in the literature for single-file studies considering age as a human factor show that it has an effect on fundamental diagrams. However, a contradictory picture of how age affects the fundamental diagram is found. One possible reason for these contradictions is that the different experiments are not comparable because even if a group is homogeneous in one factor, it could be heterogeneous in other factors such as gender. To date, only the cumulative data on all individuals in the group have been used for a comparison of the fundamental diagrams.
atoms.conditions: Cross-study single-file comparisons; age-homogeneity need not remove gender and other group/individual confounds. This is not a universal isolated age effect.

atoms.anchor_text: We collect data using three experimental settings: individual experiments with age homogeneity, single-file pedestrian experiments with age homogeneity, and single-file pedestrian experiments with age-mixed. Our findings show that age plays a substantive non-linear impact on individual unconstrained ascending and descending speeds. [...] Then, the effects of age compositions on pedestrian dynamics with fundamental diagrams (i.e., speed-density and specific flow-density relations) are analysed, and the maximum specific flow of age homogeneity is higher than that of age-mixed scenarios. Finally, we illustrate how the headway distance impacts participants’ ascending and descending speeds in both age-homogeneity and age-mixed conditions. As such, these new experimental results can provide the foundation for future calibration and validation of pedestrian evacuation models as well as insight into safety guidelines.
atoms.conditions: Stair experiments distinguish individual unconstrained walking, age-homogeneous single-file flow and mixed-age single-file flow; the abstract presents future model-calibration/validation relevance.

atoms.anchor_text: All experimental participants have no health problems and can walk independently. [...] The scenario where the single-file pedestrian flow experiment was performed in a 3.05 m × 1.5 m flight area on the stairway. A total of 11 steps connects the low-level ground and the top landing zones. [...] All volunteers could walk at normal speed on stairways and not be allowed to surpass front pedestrians.
atoms.conditions: Healthy independent walkers, a specific short stairway, normal speed and no overtaking in the single-file protocol; no unqualified transfer to mobility-impaired or emergency conditions.

core_answer_facts: [pearl-src-031a5779bd83192e] Age-related FD comparisons are not uniform and can be confounded by other group/individual characteristics.
[pearl-src-551c6f4b4febcc8a] Stair experiments distinguish individual free speed from constrained and mixed-age interactions under healthy normal-walking conditions.
[pearl-src-031a5779bd83192e; pearl-src-551c6f4b4febcc8a] Age-specific data support conditional calibration, not one universal direct speed input across settings.
reference_answer: The corpus provides documented age-specific data that can inform evacuation-model inputs, but it is not consistent enough to justify one directly transferable speed table by age. Paetzke et al. report a contradictory cross-study picture of age effects on single-file fundamental diagrams and warn that age-homogeneous groups may differ in gender or other individual factors; aggregate comparisons do not isolate age. Shi et al. separately document unconstrained ascending/descending speeds and constrained homogeneous/mixed-age single-file stair flows, finding nonlinear age effects and interaction effects in mixed populations. Their participants were healthy independent walkers on a specific stair layout, at normal speed without overtaking. Thus an individual free speed, density-constrained walking speed and mixed-stream average must not be substituted for one another, nor should stair values be assigned to level-floor motion. These data are usable as source-conditioned distributions/relations or calibration priors when the age definition, population, health/mobility, direction, geometry, density, units/statistic and processing conventions match the model. Target-condition validation and uncertainty/sensitivity remain necessary; the evidence does not establish a universal age multiplier or direct unqualified emergency-speed input.
